briefings.topic: Arvada Center Organizational & Facility Assessment — Turner Towns and Huri Report
briefings.presenter_role: National Sector Lead for Cultural Projects, Turner Towns and Huri (Turner & Townsend Hiri)
prose_paragraphs: Consultants Jenna Buer (presenting virtually) and Vicki Infenito (in person) from Turner Towns and Huri delivered findings from a roughly five-month organizational assessment of the Arvada Center for the Arts and Humanities, a city-owned facility operated by a nonprofit that is approximately 10 years old. The study was commissioned with the city's financial support and focused on four defined areas: organizational structure and staffing; performing arts programming and the presenting series; development and fundraising; and facility utilization. The methodology included on-site visits beginning in January, interviews with staff and leadership, a multi-year financial review conducted with the Center's finance team, national peer benchmarking, and facility review with architect Chris Weinman of Simple Brown Design — who provided a familiarity-based assessment of code and infrastructure considerations but did not perform a structural review. The consultants noted the Center's model is difficult to benchmark precisely because few peer organizations combine producing theater, a presenting series, extensive classes and camps, school outreach, and arts education under one roof at the same scale.

The report's overall finding was that the Arvada Center is fundamentally strong, with no critical mismanagement identified. Key data points include approximately 12,000 annual participants in classes and camps, and nearly 70,000 school children reached through bus-in and community group programs. The consultants described staffing as lean but appropriately sized, with strong retention at the mid-management-and-above level but a gap in onboarding and retention at lower levels. On the performing arts side, the main stage was identified as the primary driver of ticket revenue, and fiscal year 2026 was flagged as an exceptionally strong year — driven by productions including 'Come From Away' and 'Frozen,' the Center's 50th anniversary, and individual giving tied to the outgoing director — with a caution that FY26 should not be used as a new baseline for future projections. On the development side, the report noted that while city funding and SCFD (Scientific and Cultural Facilities District) funding remain critical, the nonprofit's 10-year fundraising history has built a diverse and growing donor base with meaningful room to grow, particularly in mid-level and corporate giving.

Consultants organized recommendations into near-term and long-term categories. Near-term priorities include: coordinating removal of the Hannes cabin from interior programming space to free up room for high-demand education classes; piloting ballroom programming using a conference room conversion; benchmarking and refining ticket pricing using dynamic pricing strategies; segmenting the mid-level donor pipeline to move donors up a 'giving ladder'; commissioning a staff compensation benchmarking study to address retention; and evaluating and implementing venue management software for operational efficiency. Longer-term recommendations include a formal, comprehensive fundraising capacity study — encompassing both annual and capital giving potential — to identify untapped donor wealth in the metro Denver area; continued rebalancing of the mainstage programming mix; protecting and growing education program earned revenue as a financial 'workhorse'; phased multi-year activation of the ballrooms as a new performance space; and building toward a strong financial reserve. A specific board evolution process was recommended, tied to the arrival of the new CEO (identified as Noel), involving mapping current board member competencies and planning succession to fill identified gaps over time. The issue of the Hannes cabin prompted an immediate comment from Councilmember Ambrose, who noted the Arvada Historical Society owns the cabin and its contents and that the society has been receiving only secondhand information about relocation plans; she indicated that she and Councilmember Lovisone, who both sit on the historical society board, would work to bring stakeholders together to find an appropriate site for the cabin.

presenter_quotes.speaker: Jenna Buer
presenter_quotes.text: We didn't find a lot of fat as it came down to it. But we also didn't find a model that was too lean. Sometimes when it's too lean, you're just not able to deliver. You're having a lot of problems. So there's a nice balance in there without being too big.
presenter_quotes.context_excerpt: We had so many discussions with staff that were saying, 'We're able to achieve this because we're being efficient in these ways. If we could grow, this is the resourcing that we would need, but we didn't find a lot of fat as it came down to it.' But we also didn't find a model that was too lean. Sometimes when it's too lean, you're just not able to deliver. You're having a lot of problems. So there's a nice balance in there without being too big.

presenter_quotes.speaker: Jenna Buer
presenter_quotes.text: You have a very talented and focused staff and organization who has come together to really make something phenomenal for this community. And they're really truly being stewards of every single dollar that they spend, every decision that they're making. And that comes through very clearly in conversations. If Philip's not in the room, they are saying the same thing that they would say when he's in the room.
presenter_quotes.context_excerpt: That's not what you have here at the Arvvada Center. You have a very talented and focused staff and organization who has come together to really make something phenomenal for this community. And they're really truly being stewards of every single dollar that they spend, every decision that they're making. And that comes through very clearly in conversations. If Philip's not in the room, they are saying the same thing that they would say when he's in the room.

presenter_quotes.speaker: Jenna Buer
presenter_quotes.text: Nobody really knows how much is possible because the data is not there. I'm a big fan of if you can show me the data and you can show me the path to get to where I need to, then we can be strategic about that and go find those resources and go find those relationships.
presenter_quotes.context_excerpt: We are recommending that there's a formal fundraising capacity study done. Nobody really knows how much is possible because the data is not there. I'm a big fan of if you can show me the data and you can show me the path to get to where I need to, then we can be strategic about that and go find those resources and go find those relationships.

presenter_quotes.speaker: Jenna Buer
presenter_quotes.text: Capital campaigns take, you know, 5 10 years sometimes within that. So they'll be able to get both answers so that then for strategic you know sort of roadmap planning they'll know both sides.
presenter_quotes.context_excerpt: It may be that as they're going through the capacity study, they say you're never going to get a capital campaign done because people are going to say X, Y, and Z. Or they may say, here's this availability for ongoing annual, but there's something really interesting here. If you would ever need to do capital, this is what this is. Capital campaigns take, you know, 5 10 years sometimes within that.

questions_raised: Whether a capital feasibility study and the recommended fundraising capacity study are the same thing, and whether the Arvada Center had previously conducted one before pausing a planned capital campaign post-pandemic.
Whether the recommended comprehensive fundraising capacity study could simultaneously assess both capital giving potential and ongoing annual giving potential, rather than requiring separate studies.
Where an economic impact study of the Arvada Center fits within the recommended scope of work, and whether such a study is already underway through the board.
Whether the Hannes cabin relocation plan is being coordinated with the Arvada Historical Society, which owns the cabin and its contents.
